# Open Christian Data - v1.0.0

OCD aims to be a single unified collection of publicly available Christian
resources. Our aim is to collate as many high quality Christian works and
resources as are available for distribution into a unified dataset for the
public good. Starting initially with a focus on works of historic significance
in the public domain.

Beyond the Bible, Christian writing is poorly represented as a cohesive dataset or as data structured for AI training. This Hugging Face release is the AI-focused publication of the collection: consistent, downloadable JSON for model training, evaluation, retrieval, and other computational uses.

**v1.0.0 — The De-slop release**

We've rebuilt the pipeline from the ground up and reprocessed every work in this release, making substantial corrections along the way. We did this so you can have much more confidence in the data you download.

**153,826,559 words across 13 categories and 881 selected editions from 852 works**, including English, Latin, and other languages. The downloads contain 711,061 records, from individual Bible verses to passages from books. Word counts measure the readable `text` fields; notes and separate introductory material are additional.

## Why the collection exists

Most public domain Christian literature beyond the Bible is scattered across
scanned books, old websites, specialist file formats, and separate
digitization projects. Even when a text is online, it may not be available as
part of a collection in which its author, work, edition, structure, and source
history are clearly preserved.

Being online is not enough. Without that context, texts are difficult to find
together, cite accurately, compare across editions, correct against their
sources, credit properly, or use responsibly in research, study, software, and
AI systems.

The collection stands on the shoulders of the faithful people who preserved,
digitized, and published these texts before us, and it stays true to their
ethos: information about Christianity and historical Christian texts should be
freely and widely available to all. Advances in AI have made a collection of
this scale practical in a way it has not been before.

## Three questions shape the data

This dataset was the project's original goal: public domain Christian text
structured for AI use. Building it raised three questions that now govern how
every record is made:

1. **Is the text a faithful copy of its source?** We keep each record linked
   to the text it was copied from, so it can be checked and corrected.
2. **Is the text a faithful copy of the original published work?** An online
   transcription may differ from the printed book. The words matter, and so do
   headings, stanzas, notes, and other features that help us read them.
3. **Is the text usable for AI?** It needs a consistent, usable format and
   clear reuse terms. We keep the source credits and terms with the text so
   you can choose what fits your project.

## What is in the collection

The [complete collection catalogue](WORK_CATALOG.md) lists all 852 works and 881 selected
copies in this release, with titles, credits, publication details, languages, source links, and download
groups. You can also download the [edition list](WORK_CATALOG.csv) or
[MODS bibliography](WORK_CATALOG.mods.xml).

The collection includes theology, church history, devotional writing, Bible translations, commentaries, sermons, creeds, catechisms, prayers, hymns, and reference works.

Representative works include Matthew Henry's *Exposition of the Old and New
Testament*, Spurgeon's *Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit*, the *Catholic
Encyclopedia*, *Nave's Topical Bible*, Augustine's *City of God*, Calvin's
*Institutes of the Christian Religion*, and editions of the *Book of Common
Prayer*.

| Kind of text | Configuration | Records | JSONL download | Arrow download |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Bible translations | `bible` | 619,210 | [598.8 MB](data/bible/train.jsonl) | [466.8 MB](data/bible/train.arrow) |
| Catechisms | `catechisms` | 1,448 | [10.9 MB](data/catechisms/train.jsonl) | [8.2 MB](data/catechisms/train.arrow) |

A record might be a verse, a sermon, a hymn, or a passage from a book. Record counts help you plan a download; they are not a count of books.

## How the collection is made

We start with a particular text and carefully make a faithful copy.

We built the Corpus Verification Workbench (CVW) so agents can visually verify their work. It lets them compare the copy with the text they copied, side by side, and check the words and layout for themselves. This also gives us readable copies for study and research.

We then build the downloadable dataset from that checked copy. If you use a passage from a book, you can still find where it belongs and read what comes before and after it. When we make a correction, we fix the copy and rebuild the downloads so the correction reaches everyone using the data.

## Using the dataset

**Using an earlier version?** Version 1.0.0 changes dataset names and fields. Follow the new configuration table and loading example when updating your code. JSONL files remain available for direct use; Hugging Face loading uses typed Arrow files.

[Read the data guide and real examples](HF_DATA_GUIDE.md), or follow the
[upgrade guide](releases/v1.0.0-migration.md) if you use an earlier version.

Install the reader, then choose a configuration:

```shell
pip install datasets
```

The release was checked with Datasets 5.1.0 and PyArrow 26.0.0.

Load it with Hugging Face Datasets:

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

texts = load_dataset(
    "OpenChristianDataOrg/open-christian-data",
    name="prose",
    split="train",
    revision="v1.0.0",
    streaming=True,
)

print(next(iter(texts))["text"])
```

Each configuration has one split, named `train`.

Pin the release tag or an immutable commit when you need to reproduce a result.

## Data structure

Use `text` for straightforward reading and processing. The other fields help you identify the text, keep passages in order, and trace them back to what was copied.

| Field | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `text` | The readable text |
| `record_id` | An identifier for this record |
| `work_id` | Which work it belongs to |
| `textual_form_id` | Which translation, revision, or other version of the work it uses |
| `edition_id` | Which edition or electronic copy is represented |
| `sequence` | The record's order |
| `locator` | Where to find this part of the text |
| `provenance` | Information about the copy and where it came from |
| `language` | The language of the text |

Some categories also provide ordered `structure`, notes, references, or introductory material. Use those fields when your task needs them: the readable text does not include every note or page marker.

Some records hold introductions, headings, or section breaks and may have empty
`text`. Different editions can also repeat passages. Check these when selecting
training or evaluation data; the [data guide](HF_DATA_GUIDE.md) has examples.

The v1 format does not carry the earlier tradition, era, audience, summary, or key-quotation fields. The generated feature definitions at the top of this card describe the fields in each configuration.

Bible references can include [OSIS](https://crosswire.org/osis/) forms such as `Gen.1.1`. Printed references remain available; supported explicit references also receive normalized forms.

## Intended uses

Open Christian Data is intended for:

- research and digital-humanities work on historical Christian writing;
- search, retrieval, reading, and reference applications;
- comparison across authors, works, periods, and traditions;
- language-model training, evaluation, retrieval augmentation, and other
  computational uses that need openly reusable Christian texts;
- building better editions or metadata by tracing records back to their
  sources and contributing corrections.

## Coverage and limitations

- Coverage varies across languages, periods, regions, and Christian traditions. The collection reflects available texts, rather than a balanced survey of Christianity.
- Historical works retain their authors' language, assumptions, disagreements, and prejudices.
- Errors may remain in the text or catalog. Please report them with a source we can check.
- Different translations and editions may contain different readings. Check which one you are using.

[Corrections and better source evidence are welcome](https://github.com/OpenChristianData/open-christian-data/issues).

[The Kingdom Collective](https://thekingdomcollective.com/spurgeon/),
[New Advent](https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/), Wikisource, and other archives
and source projects.

The hymn collection was provided by [Hymnary.org](https://hymnary.org/) at
Calvin University. If you build with it, please link to Hymnary.org and tell
them about your project through [their contact page](https://hymnary.org/contact).

[CCEL.org](https://www.ccel.org/)**, which asks to be acknowledged for making
its files available.

record the archives, digitization projects, and contributors behind the collection.

for every included text.

# A Body of Divinity: source credit and bounded text scope

Sourced via [CCEL.org](https://www.ccel.org/ccel/watson/divinity.html). The retained electronic source names Thomas Watson as author and Jon Van Hofwegen for **Markup**. Its brief CCEL staff description is by Kathleen O'Bannon; that description is outside the accepted text and the selected public rows. # A History of the Work of Redemption — source credit

Jonathan Edwards is the author identified by the retained enclosing volume, The Works of Jonathan Edwards, Volume One. This preparation represents the complete published work division, with its own preface, advertisement, general introduction, and three historical periods. Other volume works, opening matter, and combined indexes are outside this selected work. The source heading prints XIII while its native division identifier is xii; both are preserved without renumbering.

The work's preface describes posthumous publication of outlines drawn from sermons preached at Northampton in 1739. It is signed Jonathan Edwards, Newhaven, February 25, 1773, and describes the author as the signer's parent. These are distinct source-attested author and prefatory roles, despite the repeated name. The advertisement, signed John Erskine at Edinburgh, April 29, 1774, says that he reduced the original sermon form to a continued treatise and altered division marks without changing its sentiments or composition. Adalberti et Bernaldi ad Bernhardum.]`, bounded by source line identifiers `bsb00000829_00055_25` and `bsb00000829_00066_33`. Its canonical work identity calls it the Second Letter to Bernard; the source's group numbering is preserved. Other letters, the preceding shared group heading, the separately labeled fragment, and the volume shell remain in the retained source. This data represents the selected electronic witness, without independent print collation or modernization.

The source electronic publication statement applies the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license to annotations added by MGH and BSB in the DFG-funded digital MGH project. It states that the providers claim no rights in the underlying text, which they believe to be in the public domain. These are distinct source layers: the annotation license is not a new public-domain declaration for every layer or a determination for every jurisdiction. MGH and BSB request that copies and derivative versions identify both institutions as the source. This notice supplies that credit. The license reference is https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ and the project reference is https://www.dmgh.de/.

The public data is generated from the accepted TEI master and preserves ordered native content, source word annotations, line and page markers, and formatting in `structure`. The electronic header names Philip Schaff as Editor. The title's combined translation credit is retained; no finer allocation of individual tractates or extra revision role is inferred.

The complete titled source-defined collection iii consists of its own title page and all 124 tractates on the Gospel according to St. John. # Berean Standard Bible: complete retained JSON witness

Text provider: scrollmapper/bible_databases. The acquired literal marker is **BSB: Berean Standard Bible**. All 66 ordered books, 1,189 chapters and 31,102 source verse records are included, with 16 true-empty strings retained as empty verse slots. All literal leading/trailing spaces, wording, Unicode, numeric labels, IDs and order are conserved. Empty strings are not guessed, filled, omitted or interpreted as new editorial decisions. Only generated routing labels and explicit whitespace-preservation scaffolds are renewed.

The acquired JSON does not name translators, editors, publisher, print edition/date or rights holders. Separate retained openbible-io/bsb metadata associates Berean Standard Bible with **CC0-1.0** and names **BSB Publishing**. It lists **Gary Hill, Grant R. Osborne, Eugene H. Merrill, Maury Robertson, Ulrik Sandborg-Petersen and Baruch Korman** as **Advisor**, and **Gleason Archer** for **Extended translation notes**. These are precisely attributed observations of that separate metadata, not newly verified allocations to this JSON witness. Its preface names the Berean Bible Translation Committee and describes freely shareable resources. No individual role or print equivalence is inferred. The old local 2020/April 2023 claims remain historical support rather than newly confirmed source dates.

The full retained CC0 legal text below belongs to the separate openbible-io BSB repository; its metadata explicitly declares that license. The separately retained scrollmapper MIT software notice follows. Neither is silently expanded into a verified rights decision for every transformation or a claim that the spreadsheet and JSON are identical. Human acceptance, print collation, exact-witness rights review and public publication remain separate from private technical preparation.

# Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament: source and rights notice

The historical commentary is by Carl Friedrich Keil and Franz Delitzsch. English-language volumes of *Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament* were printed by T. & T. Clark in the nineteenth century, including a [1866 volume](https://books.google.com/books?id=F6NkmPGJKvIC). A [1866 Samuel volume](https://books.google.com/books?id=CKgGAAAAQAAJ) credits James Martin as translator. This example does not establish a translator assignment for every book in the electronic collection.

The accepted electronic witness was supplied by [HelloAO / AO Lab](https://bible.helloao.org/api/c/keil-delitzsch/books.json). Its retained metadata identifies this commentary text with [Public Domain Mark 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/). The mark reports public-domain status; it is not a CC0 dedication. The API software has separate terms.

The identified nineteenth-century English historical text is in the public domain in the United States. The retained electronic witness has not been collated to a particular printed exemplar, and its metadata supplies no per-book translator allocation. This disposition does not claim worldwide status for an unidentified textual or editorial layer.

## Selected source scope

The accepted witness contains 39 Old Testament book introductions, 909 chapter members, 394 chapter introductions, and 6,516 commentary occurrences. Song of Solomon has an introduction and no chapter text. Retained chapter gaps, an empty occurrence, and source attribution anomalies remain as witnessed. Private electronic routing metadata is not part of the public text rows. A complete historical printed edition is not claimed.

The item license describes the identified historical United States public-domain text and the provider-marked electronic witness.

## Current text disposition — October 9, 2026

Release row license: **Public domain (United States); historical collect text only**.

This disposition covers only source-derived historical collects and associated historical labels/rubrics. Readings, hymns, navigation, page wrappers, scripts, analytics, modern editorial wording and images are excluded. No separate grant in provider-authored material is inferred. # Charnock Volume I: source credit and scope

This private offline dataset item is the accepted Volume I portion of Stephen Charnock's *The Existence and Attributes of God*, including William Symington's life and character and the historical index and footnotes. Its two ordered records are the Volume I body and the explicitly shared two-volume apparatus. The Volume II body is outside this item and remains under its separate acceptance.

The [retained Project Gutenberg ebook 53527](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/53527) credits Richard Hulse, Colin Bell, Jonathan Cone, Alexander Bauer, and the Online Distributed Proofreading Team. The source title leaf identifies the original 1853 Robert Carter & Brothers publication, also listed in the [Robert Carter Volume I record](https://books.google.com/books/about/Discourses_Upon_the_Existence_and_Attrib.html?id=IsEGQWJPCFwC). This attribution identifies historical lineage, not a line-by-line collation to the 1853 print exemplar. The [provider's license and trademark terms](https://www.gutenberg.org/policy/license.html) remain available with the complete retained ebook.

The United States historical public-domain scope applies to the 1853 Charnock/Symington writing and historical apparatus. Factual Baker Books 1996/2000 reprint imprint details and Project Gutenberg electronic transcriber correction notes remain visible as distinct source layers; they are not represented as 1853 authored prose. A Baker website promotion is omitted from the public row, and the exact source-line-accountability JSON stays in the private inverse. The accepted master retains both. No Baker new authored introduction or design is claimed, and this item is not a verbatim Project Gutenberg ebook. This is United States private offline preparation, without a worldwide rights or public publication assertion.

# Commentary on Joshua: source credit and U.S. historical-text scope

**Sourced via [CCEL.org](https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom07/calcom07).** John Calvin wrote the commentary. Henry Beveridge translated it from the Latin and collated it with the French edition, as the retained Joshua title page states. The electronic header misspells his surname “Beverridge”; the title page, [Calvin Translation Society's 1854 annual report](https://oll-resources.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/oll3/store/titles/1793/0036_Bk_SM.pdf), and [historical catalogue](https://ndlsearch.ndl.go.jp/books/R100000136-I1971430859765009169) support “Beveridge” and the 1854 Joshua publication. The retained electronic transcription credits Ages and its markup credits sg,fj.

The dataset rows reproduce the identified historical text of the 173 explicit Commentary divisions in the accepted Joshua electronic witness. The faithful private master also retains the title page, Beveridge's preface, argument, Scripture range tables and notes, translation appendix, and indexes. Sixteen explanatory notes outside the Commentary divisions are not separate public rows. No print-exemplar collation is claimed.

**License for these rows: Public domain (United States); identified historical text and apparatus only.** The [U.S. Copyright Office's term guidance](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ15a.pdf) supplies the pre-1931 published-work basis. The shared Calvin collection catalogue says `1847 (Calvin Society)` and `Baker, 1996`; those are collection metadata, not a Joshua child-publication date or a license for 1996 additions. The modern CCEL staff description, electronic catalogue/header, cover art, images, CCEL files, and reserved formatting are excluded from these rows. The retained header's `Public Domain` statement is a provider claim; this notice makes no CC0 or worldwide-rights claim.

[CCEL's policy](https://www.ccel.org/about/copyright.html) reserves its website and special contents. The retained project permission permits parsing the underlying public-domain text and requires that CCEL files or derivatives of their formatting not be sold. Credit to CCEL here does not imply endorsement. Public deployment and rights beyond the bounded U.S. historical-text scope require separate decisions.

# Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians — source credit and United States scope

This private offline dataset follows the complete retained [Project Gutenberg eBook 1549](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1549) electronic witness of Martin Luther's *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*. The selected English text is Theodore Graebner's condensed, streamlined rendering prepared after a March 1937 publishing discussion. In his preface Graebner explicitly credits Rev. Gerhardt Mahler with the rough translation and revision on which Graebner's final draft rests. It is not presented as a literal or older English translation. Project Gutenberg credits Laura J. Hoelter and David Widger with producing the electronic text.

The nine source-defined rows retain the provider header and footer, Graebner's preface, all six chapter divisions and the full Project Gutenberg License. The retained source is a complete electronic text witness; no exact physical printing or collation is claimed.

[Project Gutenberg's eBook 1549 record](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1549) classifies this exact edition as public domain in the USA and names Graebner as translator. The selected label applies that United States classification to the identified historical Graebner/Mahler English text. The retained Project Gutenberg electronic wrapper, trademark and license text are a separate layer under the full provider license below. No independent renewal finding, CC0 dedication, worldwide clearance or public upload is asserted.

# Daily Light on the Daily Path: source and use notice

This dataset edition follows the retained CrossWire SWORD `Daily` module, version 1.0 dated January 1, 2002. Its extracted `daily.dat` and `daily.idx` supply the text and source order. The module configuration supplies metadata and rights claims. The [CrossWire module package](https://www.crosswire.org/ftpmirror/pub/sword/packages/rawzip/Daily.zip) is acquisition packaging, not the text authority. The source contains 366 ordered day entries, including February 29, with a morning and evening reading for each day. The source day labels have no year; this dataset does not assign one.

The retained module configuration titles it *Jonathan Bagster's Daily Light on the Daily Path* and credits Jonathan Bagster (1813–1872) and other members of his family. It calls the work *A Devotional Textbook for Every Day of the Year, In the Very Words of Scripture*. Separately, the retained text header says it was first published in New York by the American Tract Society around 1875. These are claims in the retained electronic source, not an independent identification or collation of an exact print edition. The retained source record attributes the SWORD module to CrossWire and records Bagster Family Bible Publishers as source context.

The module configuration states `DistributionLicense=Public Domain` and says `Public Domain -- Copy Freely`. Those are source-supplied statements. The historical compilation, its electronic arrangement, module redistribution terms, and rights in jurisdictions where that claim may not apply still require separate review before public distribution. Private offline preparation and mechanical acceptance do not establish broader rights clearance, human textual acceptance, or permission for public publication.

The public rows contain only the source-defined morning and evening readings. The 732 source Morning/Evening markers are italicized in the private TEI; the public row text retains their words but flattens that typography. Source line breaks and the literal scripture-reference text and `cRef` values remain in the rows without inferred normalized targets. The complete electronic header remains in the private accepted source representation and is excluded from public rows because it contains historical personal contact details.

# Donne, Devotions Upon Emergent Occasions

Source: the retained Project Gutenberg eBook 23772, *Devotions Upon Emergent Occasions; Together with Death's Duel*. [Project Gutenberg source](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/23772). The retained file credits Stacy Brown, John Hagerson, Juliet Sutherland, and the Online Distributed Proofreading Team (http://www.pgdp.net). Its electronic header states release December 8, 2007 and latest update December 8, 2011. The volume states First edition as an Ann Arbor Paperback 1959, University of Michigan Press; the reproduced Devotions title/imprint states London, A. M. for Thomas Iones, 1624. These retained statements do not establish physical-print equivalence.

Complete Devotions Upon Emergent Occasions in retained Project Gutenberg eBook 23772: physical lines 1481–6490, including its title/imprint, dedication, station contents, all 23 stations with Meditation, Expostulation and Prayer, and all 346 footnotes. Shared volume metadata/credits/title/imprint/contents at lines 1–92 and the explicitly Izaak Walton-attributed biographical excerpt at lines 93–1480 are front context; the complete Gutenberg terminator/license at lines 7296–7647 is back context. The volume Contents lists the biographical excerpt at roman page v; it is not a complete independent Walton Life or Donne's original Devotions body. The independently titled Death's Duel sermon (6491–7295) remains retained but is excluded from this Devotions identity. No new work identities are created; no original source bytes are removed or corrected.

The shared biographical introduction is explicitly an excerpt taken from Izaak Walton's Life of Donne and ends I.W.; its verse quotations, embedded documents and literal illustration placeholders remain source-owned context, with no invented image pixels. It is not a complete independent Life or Donne's original Devotions text. Shared volume contents and introduction do not transfer Walton authorship to Donne. Death's Duel remains unchanged in the retained source, outside this master.

The original Project Gutenberg metadata, credits, complete license and territorial notice are preserved in the TEI. The retained notice says users outside the United States must check local law. Consult the complete [Project Gutenberg License](https://www.gutenberg.org/policy/license.html) before redistribution. No independent rights clearance or publication authorization is claimed.


## Selected private US-qualified publication scope

The selected text comprises Donne's complete 1624 Devotions, the explicitly Izaak Walton-attributed historical biographical excerpt, shared volume contents and imprint facts, and the complete Gutenberg electronic license. Death's Duel is outside this accepted Devotions scope. The 1959 Ann Arbor printing is a factual imprint: the retained envelope identifies no separate modern introduction, modern editor, or permission-based copyright notice. The Walton excerpt is attributed in the retained text; it is neither a complete Life nor Donne-authored. This disposition rests on the actual historical text layers and the retained Gutenberg statement that this electronic witness is derived from text unrestricted under US copyright law, not on treating a 1959 publication date as expired.

## OpenMGH license and changes

openMGH provides its TEI-XML resources and the annotations added by the Monumenta Germaniae Historica (MGH) and the Bavarian State Library (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, BSB) under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). openMGH states that the underlying medieval text is free from copyright. Source: [openMGH](https://www.mgh.de/en/digital-mgh/openmgh). OCD reprocessed the source TEI/XML into an accepted TEI master and this public record, changing the source encoding and structure for this dataset.

# Hitchcock's Bible Names Dictionary — historical text and source credit

This U.S.-qualified private offline selection preserves all 2,622 ordered
headword and definition records of the accepted JWBickel/BibleDictionaries
electronic witness. JWBickel is credited for supplying the structured source.
Repeated Abel, Eli, Noah, and Rahab headwords remain distinct records.

Every retained headword and definition matches, in order, the identified
[CCEL historical electronic text](https://www.ccel.org/ccel/hitchcock/bible_names/bible_names.html).
Nine comparisons require only punctuation or spacing differences; their word
sequences are identical, and the retained wording is not silently edited.
The historical text contains an additional “Zuzims” entry absent from the
retained source. The selected dataset is therefore the complete accepted
electronic witness, not a complete independently collated print edition.

[CCEL's title page](https://www.ccel.org/h/hitchcock/bible_names/title.html)
identifies Roswell D. Hitchcock's names dictionary within the New York 1874
edition of *Hitchcock's New and Complete Analysis of the Holy Bible* (copyright
1869). It credits Brad Haugaard for that separate electronic text and expressly
labels it public domain. The matched historical definitions are treated as
public domain in the United States. The JWBickel source has no stated reuse
license; this notice does not invent one or transfer CCEL's electronic-text
status to JWBickel's file as a whole. The structured JSONL is credited as
provenance, while the selected definition words are supported by the complete
historical comparison.

No exact print-exemplar collation, worldwide rights, or public-upload claim is
made. The repository software license does not replace this text disposition.

# Hymnary.org selected public-domain-instance export

Hymnary.org at Calvin University provided this oldest-PD-instances export for inclusion in Open Christian Data, received April 22, 2026. The retained acquisition record describes each record as the oldest known public-domain hymnal instance for that hymn text and labels this specific export public domain. This provider designation is the basis for private offline preparation of this collection. It is not a claim about every resource on Hymnary.org or an independent rights determination for every underlying text, translation, edition, or jurisdiction.

**Provider credit and requested acknowledgment:** link to [Hymnary.org](https://hymnary.org) when using this dataset. Application developers are encouraged to [submit their projects through Hymnary's contact page](https://hymnary.org/contact). No contact has been sent as part of this preparation.

The accepted retained CSV contains **34,895 source records**, with eight fields in original order. The historical generated collection has 34,904 entries and is a separate artifact, not reconstruction authority. The CSV is the textual source; its ZIP is only a transport package. This collection is a supplied export, not a claim to complete or critically edited hymn editions.

All author and date strings remain provider-supplied values, including blanks, uncertain wording, and dates of later hymnals. A later hymnal printing date does not establish when its hymn text or translation originated. The source contains 31,796 records with literal hymnal years before 1931 and 3,099 records with later or uncertain hymnal years; this census is not newly verified publication dating or a row-level legal review. The provider's selected-export designation covers the supplied collection, rather than being inferred from those dates.

The faithful reconstruction preserves original spelling, source order, empty fields, repeated titles, line breaks, and literal backslashes. Seven nonstandard quotation occurrences remain unresolved. Fifteen XML-forbidden source controls are represented by visible labeled glyph placeholders. No stanza divisions, author identities, or publication dates have been inferred or corrected.

The website's [general copyright information](https://hymnary.org/copyright) describes both public-domain and reserved resources. That general notice does not replace the specific supplied-export designation; it also does not grant use of other website text, tunes, images, or resources. This private preparation performs no public upload and makes no worldwide clearance claim.

# Hymnus de gloriosissimo Christi martyre Gangulfo

Source and digital annotations: Monumenta Germaniae Historica (MGH) and the Bavarian State Library, Munich (BSB), through digital MGH, funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG).

The electronic witness is the openMGH TEI-XML volume bsb00000754, representing Passiones vitaeque sanctorum aevi Merovingici (V), Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum volume 7, edited by Bruno Krusch, published by Hahn, Hannover, 1920. See the [openMGH TEI-XML volume list](https://www.mgh.de/en/digital-mgh/openmgh/mgh-editions-in-openmgh). The electronic publication statement is dated November 28, 2016.

The source declares its added annotations available under [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) and claims no rights on the text itself, which it believes to be public domain. This derivative preserves the electronic hymn's native wording, mixed text, line markers, and two column spans in a work-specific faithful TEI, then projects the accepted master to native poetry data. Credit MGH and BSB when distributing copies or derivatives.

The hymn comprises five numbered stanzas ending with Amen. The separately titled following Vita is excluded. The literal source heading is “[HYMNUS DE GLORIOSISSIMO CHRISTI MARTIRE GENGULFO.”; its closing bracket occurs in the following Vita heading. No closing bracket or corrected spelling has been added. The source reading “Cleinenterque” remains unchanged. The catalog title above serves as the existing work identity label; it is not a claim that the source heading was spelled identically.

This is a technically checked reconstruction of the entire retained electronic hymn. Print collation, close visual comparison, human review, independent rights clearance, and publication authorization remain separate and unrecorded.

# Jerome Letters: source and data credit

Sourced via [CCEL.org](https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf206.html), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, volume VI, edited by Philip Schaff and Henry Wace. The title page names W. H. Fremantle, assisted by G. Lewis and W. G. Martley. In the Translator's Preface, Fremantle says Lewis and Martley prepared the first draft and added most notes, while he reviewed every part, correcting, adding and sometimes rewriting manuscript/proofs, and composed Prolegomena and Indices. These are source-attested volume roles; no unsupported per-letter allocation is inferred.

The electronic printSourceInfo states New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892. The retained title page names T&T Clark, Edinburgh, and Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing Company, Grand Rapids, Michigan. Fremantle signs Canterbury, November, 1892. These distinct source claims remain separate; no print-equivalence or date correction is inferred.

The electronic header states Public Domain and identifies Christian Classics Ethereal Library as electronic publisher. Retained CCEL permission permits parsing ThML/XML for text, reserves CCEL file/formatting rights and restricts selling CCEL files or derivatives of their formatting. Credit CCEL when publishing. Provider statements are not independent rights clearance.

Complete retained CCEL NPNF2-06 ThML.body/div1[@id='v'], The Letters of St. Jerome, all 150 source-numbered entries, including translated text, abstracts, incoming correspondence and disputed attributions exactly as supplied. This is the complete retained editorial collection, not 150 fully translated letters all authored by Jerome. All 13,459 native elements, 151 literal heads, 4,012 notes, 295 page markers, and 2,853 source scripRef tags, six explicitly neutral letter references and five Hebrew RTL spans are preserved. Shared title pages/Translator's Preface/Prolegomena and indexes remain separately accounted retained context; relevant primary credits are localized in header/notices. All nine sibling treatises remain outside this master. One collection, one TEI; no child work identities, invented missing text or corrected source readings.

Source headings preserve correspondents and disputed attribution; some numbered entries are only abstracts, including CXLVIII through CL, whose source explicitly qualifies non-Jerome authorship. Full omitted compositions are not invented. Historical treatise-only helpers' suggestion of constituent work IDs is not adopted for this explicitly authorized complete collection identity. Human textual/visual acceptance, print collation, rights clearance and publication remain separate. Carry visible credit to `data/prose/jerome-letters/README.md`.

# John Chrysostom â€” Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles

This text is sourced via CCEL.org: [Christian Classics Ethereal Library](https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf111.html), *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers*, First Series, volume XI. The Acts title page credits translation with notes and indices to J. Walker, J. Sheppard, and H. Browne, with revision and additional notes by George B. Stevens. Philip Schaff is series editor. The Oxford Part I preface, signed C. Marriott in 1851, credits Walker and Sheppard's earlier translation and Browne's restoration, correction, retranslation, and prefatory matter. Stevens signs the American preface in March 1889. Retained printSourceInfo states Edinburgh: T&T Clark, without a print date; the title page also names Wm. B. Eerdmans. No reprint date is inferred.

The complete source-defined Acts collection contains fifty-five homilies and introductory carriers: 10,930 native source elements, including 1,181 notes, 332 page markers, 2,446 scripture references, and 55 scripture-commentary carriers. Complete wording, headings, hierarchy, Greek and Hebrew, inline tails, note attachments, page links, reference annotations, and the closing prayer remain within one TEI. The 1,064 source elements without IDs retain their historical generated identities. Two right-to-left spans retain their source direction through explicit rendition tokens. The independently titled Romans work, shared title pages, prefaces, and indexes remain in immutable source context outside the Acts body; their relevant credits and editorial policies are recorded here and in the TEI header.

The Oxford and American prefaces describe imperfect unrevised sermon reports, uncertain passages, conjectural emendations and transpositions. The American revision also reports limited phraseology changes, Revised Version and critical-text substitutions, small annotation omissions, and imperfect reference adaptation. These are the retained edition's editorial statements. OCD does not silently repair those readings or claim independent printed completeness, print collation, authorship adjudication, or correctness of electronic passage/OSIS parsing and versification. The retained electronic text was reconstructed as one TEI and projected as ordered native content into JSONL and Arrow.

The retained electronic header states Public Domain for the text. Separate retained CCEL permission evidence permits parsing, reserves CCEL file and formatting rights, and restricts selling CCEL files or derivatives of their formatting. These distinct layers are preserved as evidence; they do not establish independent rights clearance or suitability for a selected public release profile. Visible attribution follows the retained instruction to say sourced via CCEL.org.

This private offline technical rehearsal does not establish new visual review, human acceptance, print collation, independent rights clearance, global release selection, or publication authorization.

# John Chrysostom — Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews

This text is sourced via CCEL.org: [Christian Classics Ethereal Library](https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf114.html), *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers*, First Series, volume XIV. Philip Schaff is series editor. The work's own Preface credits T. Keble as Oxford translator and his brother, the Vicar of Hursley, as reviser. Dr. Barrow later revised the translation against Field's Greek text and supplied headings. P. E. Pusey signs the Oxford preface, May 1877, and responsibility for occasional bracketed notes. The own title page credits Frederic Gardiner with revising the Oxford translation, Introduction, and notes; he is not credited here as the original translator. A posthumous note is signed F.G., jr.; Schaff's shared preface states that Gardiner's son read the proofs. No unrecorded full name or individual contributor assignment is inferred.

The retained printSourceInfo states Edinburgh: T&T Clark, with no print date; the series title page also names Wm. B. Eerdmans Publishing Company. May 1877 is the signed Oxford preface date and December 1889 the signed Schaff preface date, not independently established dates of this printed witness. No print collation or reprint identity is claimed.

The complete source-defined Hebrews collection contains thirty-eight divisions: its own Title Page, Preface, Introduction, Argument, and thirty-four homilies. All 6,035 native source elements remain together as one TEI, including 881 notes, 181 page markers, 1,190 reference carriers, 34 commentary carriers, nineteen source line breaks, Greek and inline mixed text/tails. All 243 source elements without IDs retain their historical generated identities using global ordinal offset 52832. The exact final paragraph is v.xxxviii-p76, Thanks be to God. The independently titled John collection and shared volume title, Schaff preface, comparative table, and indexes remain outside this body in immutable source context. Their relevant credits and policies are recorded here and in the TEI header. OCD reconstructed the entire Hebrews collection as one TEI and projected its ordered native content into JSONL and Arrow.

The complete own Preface preserves editorial/transmission claims about posthumously published sermon notes by Constantine or Constantius, older and polished textual forms, manuscript and Latin-version evidence, Field's editorial restoration, and headings. Gardiner's revision states that A.V. is the scriptural standard with exceptions and material R.V. variations, that language was simplified and some prior translations reversed, and that English notes were retained with bracketed initialed additions. The Introduction disputes Pauline authorship assumed in Chrysostom's Argument. These are retained editorial statements, not independent adjudication or permission to silently repair readings. The inherited mapping of scripRef to ref type=scripture describes the electronic source carrier, including non-Biblical Ep. citations in the Preface. It does not establish Biblical identification, electronic parsing, or versification correctness.

The retained electronic header states Public Domain for the text. Separate retained CCEL permission evidence permits parsing, reserves CCEL file and formatting rights, and restricts selling CCEL files or derivatives of their formatting. These distinct layers are preserved as evidence; they do not establish independent rights clearance or suitability for a selected public release profile. Visible attribution follows the instruction to say sourced via CCEL.org.

Historical review ticket 37a-09 provides bounded native visual observations, including corrected exact terminal evidence, with explicit invalid older-route limitations. Its receipts are historical context; no new pixels, whole-word proofreading, print collation, human acceptance, independent rights clearance, global release selection, or publication authorization is claimed by this private offline preparation.

# King James Version: retained electronic verse-text notice

This private, U.S.-qualified preparation contains the 66 ordered books, 1,189 chapters, and 31,102 verse strings of the existing accepted KJV electronic witness from [Scrollmapper bible_databases](https://github.com/scrollmapper/bible_databases). Each retained verse object has only `verse` and `text` fields. The source translation marker mentions Strong's numbers, morphology, and catchwords, but none is present in the retained verse objects or represented as extra public content. Source strings and boundaries remain unchanged. The marker calls the version “1769”; it does not prove exact collation to a particular Blayney printing or the identity of later electronic editors.

The historical King James Version wording was published in 1611 and its commonly labeled 1769 form long before the current [U.S. copyright term cutoff](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ15a.pdf). The qualified U.S. public-domain statement here concerns that historical wording and source-derived verse positions, not every right in the electronic file, later apparatus, or other territories. [Cambridge University Press identifies U.K. Crown-patentee rights](https://assets.cambridge.org/97805211/63347/copyright/9780521163347_copyright_info.pdf) in the Authorized Version; U.K. and global distribution are not asserted by this private preparation.

The provider's [KJV-specific source notice](https://github.com/scrollmapper/bible_databases/blob/master/sources/en/KJV/README.md), preserved in our rights research, labels its electronic translation **GPL** without stating a version. GNU GPLv3 section 14 permits the recipient to choose a Free Software Foundation-published GPL version when the covered work states none. For any protectable contribution to the selected electronic verse data, this private preparation elects GNU GPLv3 and preserves the provider's exact unversioned label. The complete, unmodified GPLv3 text is delivered in the paired data notice as a literal text block. The separately reviewed [CrossWire KJV module](https://www.crosswire.org/sword/modules/ModInfo.jsp?modName=KJV) uses the same full KJV/1769/Strong's/morphology/catchwords title, labels module distribution GPL, credits Bible Foundation, Project KJV2003, Dr. Maurice Robinson, and Michael Paul Johnson for electronic work, and grants use of CrossWire's KJV2003 text for any purpose. The matching title supports related provenance, but the retained Scrollmapper JSON does not itself prove a complete derivation chain from a particular CrossWire module revision. This notice does not silently replace the provider's GPL label with CrossWire's grant.

The retained Scrollmapper repository carries the following MIT notice for its software and associated documentation. We preserve it in full; we do not treat it as a blanket license for the Bible translation or all electronic data. The selected public rows consist of verse wording and mechanical book/chapter/verse locations; repository software, JSON packaging, modern module apparatus, and unselected website material are not delivered as text content. Provider and electronic-source credit remain visible. This private preparation is not public upload authorization.

MIT License

Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy
of this software and associated documentation files (the "Software"), to deal
in the Software without restriction, including without limitation the rights
to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell
copies of the Software, and to permit persons to whom the Software is

The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all

THE SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED "AS IS", WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, EXPRESS OR

AUTHORS OR COPYRIGHT HOLDERS BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM, DAMAGES OR OTHER

OUT OF OR IN CONNECTION WITH THE SOFTWARE OR THE USE OR OTHER DEALINGS IN THE
SOFTWARE.

The selected UTF-8 JSONL records are a directly editable form of the delivered verse text: each record contains the wording and its source-derived book, chapter, verse, and order. There is no compiled or binary form in this selected Bible configuration. The change from the provider's JSON is structural representation through accepted TEI and public JSONL; verse strings and their order are not edited. The original provider JSON is linked from the source credit above. This license copy is for any protectable electronic contribution; it does not turn the historical U.S. public-domain words into a newly owned work.

The last sermon is XCV, A Homily on the Beatitudes, St. Matt. v. 1-9; its full closing doxology and Amen remain, with the final notes attached. The independently titled Gregory collection and shared volume title/indexes remain outside Leo in immutable retained context. No new per-letter or per-sermon work IDs are created.

He credits Canon Bright's *S. complete first and second volumes of Olaudah Equiano's *The Interesting
Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano: or Gustavus Vassa, the African.

Text Creation Partnership (TCP) ECCO electronic transcription. Volume 1 has

# Open English Bible: source and rights notice

Open English Bible project, [official release 2025.6](https://openenglishbible.org/oeb/2025.6/), US and Commonwealth spelling variants.

The project releases its translation under [CC0 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/). This dedication permits redistribution and adaptation without an attribution condition; source credit is retained for identification.

## Electronic witness scope

Official Open English Bible 2025.6 US and Commonwealth-spelling branches: 44 biblical books in each variant, comprising 17 selected Old Testament books and the full 27-book New Testament. This is a partial Bible.

The text is represented as structured dataset records. Source wording, retained numbering and known omissions remain distinguished from generated routing. Completeness of a historical printed edition is not implied.

Public row license: `cc0-1.0`, for the provider-declared electronic text route described above. Separate software notices retain their stated scope.

# Original Douay-Rheims: retained structured electronic witness

Source: the pinned v1.0 release of janvier-s/original-douay-rheims. The actual extracted tagged JSON, annotation sidecars and reference documents are textual authorities; the ZIP is a package. Raw JSON and USFM derivatives remain retained and accounted separately.

Primary title documents credit the English College of Rheims and the English College of Doway. Gregory Martin and contemporary revisers/annotators are retained configuration attributions; no finer role allocation is inferred. The release README describes original 1582 New Testament and 1609–1610 Old Testament translation. Literal New Testament title material also states a fourth edition in 1633; Old Testament title material also carries 1635. These provider and title statements do not establish independent printed-witness identity or full collation.

The complete retained electronic collection includes 73 canonical books and three appendix components; two Prayer filenames are an exact duplicate, accounted once. The inherited historical Catholic reading order is generated and explicitly declared, not literal archive order. All 37,181 source verse occurrences and 4,776,267 literal visible verse characters are retained, including both Tobias chapter-zero carriers and the duplicate native address. No verse is silently dropped, renumbered or assigned an invented normalized reference.

Nine source chapter articles and their 440 subnotes, omitted by the historical producer, are restored. Seventy-three absent JSON-null language-title fields are explicitly typed as source absence, not displayed as an authored title. The rest of the historical body is retained through an exact reversible inverse. Complete nonverse context, source locators, inline structures, text/tails and annotation relationships are delivered in numbered annex parts generated from the actual TEI. JSON string escapes and numbered fragments retain exact literal spaces and comparison characters; generated labels are explanatory, not source-supplied IDs or newly authored footnotes.

The retained README and LICENSE declare CC0 1.0 Universal and say attribution is not required. This is provider evidence, not independent worldwide rights clearance. Human textual/visual acceptance, print collation, rights clearance and public publication remain separate.

# Orthodoxy: source credit and rights

Electronic source: [Standard Ebooks](https://github.com/standardebooks/g-k-chesterton_orthodoxy). Open Christian Data reformatted the retained electronic witness into TEI and a structured public-text projection. Any encoded gaps remain; no new translation or claim of print collation is made.

Colophon Colophon Orthodoxy was published in 1908 by G. K. Chesterton. This ebook was produced for Standard Ebooks by Justin Disney, and is based on a transcription produced in 2005 by Jonathan Ingram, Clare Coney, and Distributed Proofreaders for Project Gutenberg and on digital scans from the Internet Archive. The cover page is adapted from Christ Healing the Blind, a painting completed in 1570 by El Greco. The cover and title pages feature the League Spartan and Sorts Mill Goudy typefaces created in 2014 and 2009 by The League of Moveable Type. The first edition of this ebook was released on April 26, 2021, 9:21 p.m. You can check for updates to this ebook, view its revision history, or download it for different ereading systems at standardebooks.org/ebooks/g-k-chesterton/orthodoxy. The volunteer-driven Standard Ebooks project relies on readers like you to submit typos, corrections, and other improvements. Anyone can contribute at standardebooks.org.

The source writing is identified by Standard Ebooks as public domain in the United States. Contributors dedicate their ebook contributions under [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/). That dedication does not change the source writing's status in other countries. This notice makes no worldwide source-text grant and does not cover separately selected image assets.

The OPF reports a 1910 A. W. Verity basis and HathiTrust digital scans; no independent print collation confirms that basis. The poem's 1667 original publication and the 2019 Standard Ebooks digital release are distinct dates. The local config's language and contributor omissions do not override the retained OPF.

# Practical Mysticism: source credit and rights

Colophon Colophon Practical Mysticism was published in 1914 by Evelyn Underhill. This ebook was produced for Standard Ebooks by Steven McCurdy, and is based on a transcription produced in 2007 by Ruth Hart and Distributed Proofreaders for Project Gutenberg and on digital scans from the Internet Archive. The cover page is adapted from The Transfiguration, a painting completed between 1518 and 1520 by Raphael. The cover and title pages feature the League Spartan and Sorts Mill Goudy typefaces created in 2014 and 2009 by The League of Moveable Type. The first edition of this ebook was released on October 30, 2019, 8:22 p.m. You can check for updates to this ebook, view its revision history, or download it for different ereading systems at standardebooks.org/ebooks/evelyn-underhill/practical-mysticism. The volunteer-driven Standard Ebooks project relies on readers like you to submit typos, corrections, and other improvements. Anyone can contribute at standardebooks.org.

The source writing is identified by Standard Ebooks as public domain in the United States. Green, 1772; Evans 12494). Credit: Samson Occom; Text Creation Partnership, N09814; https://name.umdl.umich.edu/N09814.0001.001 and https://github.com/textcreationpartnership/N09814. TCP respectfully requests credit to the original source.

The retained provider header offers its Phase I keyboarded and encoded text under Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal. The complete retained CC0 legal code follows. Commercial Readex/Newsbank page images are not included or licensed by this text notice. The public row is a readable projection of the accepted text: notes and page markers remain in ordered structure; readable text omits them. The retained 17 illegible gaps remain visible as source uncertainty. Human review, page-image collation, project rights clearance, and public publication are separate decisions.

# Savoy Declaration of Faith: source and rights notice

The historical English declaration dates to 1658. This release reproduces the accepted Creeds.json electronic witness: thirty-two chapters and 159 sections. It is not a facsimile, a new translation, or a claim of complete historical print collation. The separately published preface and platform of church order are outside this retained member.

Sourced through [NonlinearFruit/Creeds.json](https://github.com/NonlinearFruit/Creeds.json). The retained member explicitly credits **Copyright - Reformed Standards** and links [Reformed Standards compendium, Savoy source](https://github.com/reformed-standards/compendium/blob/master/data/british/savoy.yaml). The upstream compendium grants [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/reformed-standards/compendium/blob/c2f698ed3deaa50687b6dc1b14b4dbf71cb44fd8/LICENSE) for its contributions. Preserve this separate electronic-source grant and attribution; Creeds.json’s general Unlicense does not replace this member exception. The historical text is public domain in the United States; no CC0 dedication is asserted.

Modification and scope notice: Creeds.json converts the upstream YAML to its own JSON chapter/section structure, omits inline reference-letter markers and upstream proof-reference lists, and supplies its metadata. OCD reconstructs the retained member in TEI and projects its native ordered text; the original source and accepted master remain unchanged. A comparison of every retained section with the identified current upstream found 158 matching texts after whitespace and reference-marker normalization. Chapter 1, section 2 in the retained witness omits “2 Corinthians” from the Bible-book list. This known source omission is reproduced faithfully and disclosed; the release does not claim that this list is complete. No silent repair or substitution of the current upstream was performed.

No images, website design, upstream YAML files, or unretained apparatus are included. This is private offline release preparation; it does not authorize public upload or establish worldwide historical-text rights. The full applicable upstream license follows.

# Second Epitaph for Georgius, from Epitaphium senioris Georgii triplex

Source: Monumenta Germaniae Historica (MGH) and Bavarian State Library, Munich (BSB), [openMGH MGH SS rer. Germ. 73](https://www.dmgh.de/mgh_ss_rer_germ_73/index.htm). The retained volume bibliography credits Bernhard Vogel and gives Hannover: Hahn, 2001. These volume statements do not establish print equivalence or stronger attribution to this individual poem.

The literal source ALIUD heading introduces this complete second six-line epitaph. It belongs to the three-poem EPITAPHIUM SENIORIS GEORGII TRIPLEX collection. The collection heading is context; the first and third poems are excluded. This preparation represents one complete independent epitaph and does not claim to represent the whole triplex. The source Carmina heading reads Versus fratris Lamberti in monasterio sancti Laurentii; that statement remains collection context. Native line identifiers, spelling, punctuation and the internal page break are preserved.

The electronic header licenses MGH/BSB annotations under [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) and does not claim rights in the underlying text, which it believes to be public domain. Credit MGH and BSB when distributing copies or derivatives. Human verification, visual review, print comparison, final rights disposition and publication authorization remain separate.

# Select Orations: source credit

This English text is John of Damascus, “Sermon II. On the Assumption,” translated by Mary H. Allies in *St John Damascene on Holy Images. Followed by Three Sermons on the Assumption* (London: Thomas Baker, 1898). The retained electronic witness is [Project Gutenberg eBook 49917](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49917), produced by Andrew Dunning. # Source and rights notice for The Epistle of Ignatius to the Magnesians

This electronic text comes from [Project Gutenberg eBook 77576](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/77576), *The Writings of the Apostolic Fathers* (T. & T. Clark, Edinburgh, 1870). The retained extracted HTML supplies the complete source-titled Magnesians letter at direct body children `[464,544)`, including the salutation, chapters I–XV with paired shorter and longer Greek readings, 13 printed page markers, and 96 linked source notes `f890`–`f985`. The ZIP is the acquisition package. Other titled works and shared volume matter are outside this selection; no shared Syriac manuscript notice is selected.

## Current historical-text disposition — October 9, 2026

For *The Epistle of Ignatius to the Trallians* (`pg77576-ignatius-trallians`), the current release row license is **Public domain (United States and Australia); 1870 historical text, translation, and notes only**. This item-specific disposition supersedes only the earlier preliminary statement that rights in the selected 1870 translation, textual edition and linked historical notes remained unassessed.

The selected literary text and notes derive from T. & T. Clark, Edinburgh, 1870. Alexander Roberts died in 1901, James Donaldson in 1915, and Frederick Crombie before 1890. The historical publication and corroborated pre-1955 deaths support this text route in the United States and Australia. The existing collective translation credits and uncertainty about individual passage assignments remain unchanged; the Hermas Similitudes attribution to Crombie is preserved where applicable.

This assessment covers only this accepted constituent’s historical text, translation, introduction and linked 1870 notes. # Source and rights notice for The Epistle of Ignatius to the Virgin Mary

This text was prepared from [Project Gutenberg eBook 77576](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/77576), *The Writings of the Apostolic Fathers*. The electronic edition credits David King and the Online Proofreading Team at PGDP; its source images were made available by the Internet Archive. The volume names Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and Frederick Crombie as translators; the title page identifies Roberts and Donaldson as editors, without assigning this letter to one translator. Its appendix labels the additional Ignatian letters spurious.

# Source and rights notice for The Epistle of Polycarp

This electronic text is Polycarp’s *Epistle to the Philippians* from [Project Gutenberg eBook 77576](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/77576), *The Writings of the Apostolic Fathers* (T. & T. Clark, Edinburgh, 1870). The retained extracted HTML supplies this constituent’s introductory notice, 14 chapter headings, 80 linked source footnotes, and 12 source page markers (65 and 67–77). # Source and rights notice for The Epistle to Diognetus

This text was reconstructed from [Project Gutenberg eBook 77576](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/77576), *The Writings of the Apostolic Fathers* (Ante-Nicene Christian Library, volume I; Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1870). Its introductory notice calls the epistle anonymous; the title page names Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson as editors and lists Roberts, Donaldson, and Frederick Crombie as translators. The editors' note attributes the volume translation to Roberts and Donaldson except for the *Similitudes of Hermas*, translated by Crombie; it does not identify which editor translated this epistle. ## Current historical-text disposition — October 9, 2026

For *The Pastor of Hermas* (`pg77576-pastor-hermas`), the current release row license is **Public domain (United States and Australia); 1870 historical text, translation, and notes only**. This item-specific disposition supersedes only the earlier preliminary statement that rights in the selected 1870 translation, textual edition and linked historical notes remained unassessed.

The selected literary text and notes derive from T. & T. Clark, Edinburgh, 1870. Alexander Roberts died in 1901, James Donaldson in 1915, and Frederick Crombie before 1890. The historical publication and corroborated pre-1955 deaths support this text route in the United States and Australia. The existing collective translation credits and uncertainty about individual passage assignments remain unchanged; the Hermas Similitudes attribution to Crombie is preserved where applicable.

# Source and rights notice for The Second Epistle of Clement

This text was prepared from [Project Gutenberg eBook 77576](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/77576), *The Writings of the Apostolic Fathers*. The volume was originally published in Edinburgh by T. & T. Clark in 1870. Its title page names Rev. Dr. Roberts, Dr. Donaldson, and Rev. F. Crombie as translators. The editors' note says the volume was translated by its editors except for the *Similitudes of Hermas*; it does not identify one translator for this work. The source's introductory notice disputes Clement's authorship and reports that some critics view the text as a homily, so the source title is retained without asserting Clement as author.

Project Gutenberg credits David King and the Online Proofreading Team at PGDP for the electronic edition and states that it was produced from images made available by the Internet Archive. The [Project Gutenberg license](https://www.gutenberg.org/license) accompanies its eBook, and the [eBook page](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/77576) links to the original electronic formats. Any selected release must preserve the applicable license terms and access to an original format.

# The Existence and Attributes of God, Volume 2

This offline dataset contains the accepted Volume 2 discourse text and the shared two-volume index, footnotes, and transcriber notes from the retained electronic witness of Stephen Charnock's *The Existence and Attributes of God*. A separate Volume 1 work covers the first volume. The public text omits only private source-line bookkeeping; the accepted master and retained source preserve it. The Project Gutenberg ebook wrapper and license are outside this work's text scope.

The historical Volume 2 text is associated with the 1853 New York Robert Carter edition, corroborated by the [Princeton Theological Seminary Library scan](https://archive.org/details/discoursesupone02char). This electronic transcription has not been collated line by line to that print exemplar. The shared electronic transcriber notes are identified as factual correction apparatus rather than Charnock's prose.

Source: [Project Gutenberg ebook 53527](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/53527), with production credits to Richard Hulse, Colin Bell, Jonathan Cone, Alexander Bauer, and the Online Distributed Proofreading Team. [Project Gutenberg license and trademark terms](https://www.gutenberg.org/policy/license.html). This is an acknowledgment of the retained source, not an assertion that the offline rows reproduce the branded ebook.

Rights scope: historical 1853 text and apparatus for private United States offline preparation. The source catalog labels the ebook public domain in the United States; [U.S. Copyright Office duration guidance](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ15a.pdf) supports the historical publication basis. This notice makes no worldwide, exact-print, human-acceptance, or public-publication claim.

# The First Book of Samuel — source and rights notice

This commentary is W. G. Blaikie's *The First Book of Samuel*, part of *The Expositor's Bible*, edited by William Robertson Nicoll. The retained electronic text was sourced via CCEL.org. Its primary title page names Toronto, Willard Tract Depository and Bible Depot, 1888; the electronic metadata literally spells “Williard,” and both source readings have been retained.

This release selection covers the separately titled First Samuel electronic witness, including its title page, chapters I–XXXVI, and indexes. It does not include Blaikie's *The Second Book of Samuel*, Blaikie's *The Book of Joshua*, the whole Expositor's Bible series, or a claim of printed-edition collation.

The retained source labels its underlying text “Public Domain.” The complete retained CCEL permission statement is: “Confirmed 2026-04-01 by Quincy (CCEL): parsing ThML/XML files for text is explicitly permitted. CCEL's copyright applies to their files and formatting only — not the underlying PD texts. Restriction: do not sell CCEL files or derivatives of their formatting. # The Life of Constantine with Orations: source credit

Sourced via [CCEL.org](https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf201.html), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, volume I, Eusebius Pamphilus. Its own title page credits Ernest Cushing Richardson with revised translation, prolegomena and notes for the Life of Constantine together with Constantine's Oration to the Saints and Eusebius's Oration in Praise of Constantine. His signed Preface describes revision of the Bagster translation and is dated Hartford, April 15, 1890. The collection preserves these different attributed works as the accepted source-defined selection; it does not assign Constantine's oration to Eusebius. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace are the series editors.

The electronic printSourceInfo states New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1890. These are source bibliographic statements, without inferred print collation or metadata correction.

The electronic header states Public Domain. Retained CCEL permission allows parsing ThML, requests CCEL.org credit, reserves CCEL file/formatting rights and restricts selling CCEL files or derivatives of their formatting. These provider statements do not establish independent rights clearance.

Complete source-native ThML.body/div1[@id='iv'] (The Life of Constantine with Orations of Constantine and Eusebius.) only from npnf201; top-level sibling roots i, ii, iii, v, vi remain outside this accepted constituent selection.

Human/print review, rights clearance, global selection and public publication remain separate.

# The Solemn League and Covenant — historical text and electronic witness

This U.S.-qualified private offline dataset includes four historical units from the accepted electronic witness: the title and scriptural preamble; the August 17, 1643 Edinburgh General Assembly approval; the July 15, 1644 Scottish Parliament act; and the Covenant, including historical references through 1651. The historical text and acts are treated as public domain in the United States. [The Westminster Standard](https://thewestminsterstandard.org/the-solemn-league-and-covenant/) is credited as the provider of the retained electronic witness.

The selected records preserve the accepted HTML transcription's wording and source order, including apparent “Assemblyxs” and “Majestyxs” anomalies. A [1643 Edinburgh print record](https://quod.lib.umich.edu/cgi/i/idresolver/idresolver-nr?id=B05905.0001.001) and [Edinburgh-edition comparison text](https://media.acny.uk/media/venues/page/attachment/2022/08/The_Westminster_Confession_of_Faith.pdf) corroborate the old document and act scope; they are not the accepted source and this release does not claim exact print-exemplar collation.

Two historical heading strings were carried inside HTML accordion links and plus-sign icons. Their words remain; only the electronic link/icon wrappers and two target references are omitted reversibly from public rows. The retained page's “© 2016” and “© 2026” website footers are outside these selected rows. Those site-layer notices do not determine rights in the seventeenth-century wording and do not authorize reuse of the whole website. No modern authored commentary is selected. This disposition makes no U.K. or worldwide rights claim and does not authorize public upload.

The first edition of this ebook was released on April 8, 2025, 4:07 p.m. You can check for updates to this ebook, view its revision history, or download it for different ereading systems at standardebooks.org/ebooks/george-macdonald/unspoken-sermons. # World Messianic Bible — source and reuse

This selected text is the retained [eBible World Messianic Bible](https://ebible.org/engwmb) USFM electronic witness. The source copyright page labels it an August 2022 stable text using U.S. spelling; the retained support HTML also names its own later generation date. The accepted scope is the complete ordered 66-book USFM text, with 31,103 verse carriers and no FRT or GLO member. The ZIP package and its three nontext support members are retained source support, not additional public verse text.

The public text selection consists of verse rows. The accepted private master also retains book-level headings, source markers, and three notes outside verse rows. Source-native identifiers are not claims of normalized cross-edition Bible references.

The following is the complete copyright and permissions wording in the two rights paragraphs of the retained copr.htm, with whitespace normalized for display:

The World Messianic Bible is not copyrighted, however "World Messianic Bible" is a Trademark.

You may copy, publish, proclaim, distribute, redistribute, sell, give away, quote, memorize, read publicly, broadcast, transmit, share, back up, post on the Internet, print, reproduce, preach, teach from, and use the World Messianic Bible as much as you want, and others may also do so. All we ask is that if you CHANGE the actual text of the World Messianic Bible in any way, you not call the result the World Messianic Bible any more. This is to avoid confusion, not to limit your freedom. The Holy Bible is God's Word. It belongs to God. He gave it to us freely, and we who have worked on this translation freely give it to you by dedicating it to the Public Domain.

# Summa Theologica: four-component source and data credit

The retained title and imprint identify Thomas Aquinas, translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province, Complete American Edition, Benziger Brothers, New York.
